notesStmt.note: In a letter to Richard Maurice Bucke, dated November 4, 1888, Whitman notes that was in the process of working on a "short concluding note at end" for what he was calling "the big book." On November 10, Whitman wrote that he had "finished the little beginning & end Notes I spoke of for the big book and sent to the printer." This aligns with the date written at the bottom of the present manuscript, meaning that it was almost certainly composed in early November of 1888 and completed by November 10.
A manuscript draft of "Note at end of Complete Poems and Prose," published in Complete Poems & Prose (1888–9).

body.p:
As I conclude—and (to get typographical correctness,) after running ‸my eyes diligently through the three big divisions of the preceding Volume—the ‸interrogative wonder⹀‸⹀fancy rises in me whether (if it be not too arrogant to ‸even claim state it,) the 38 33 years of this my current time, 18505–1888, with their aggregate of our New World history doings & people, have not ‸really created and formulatedformulated the foregoing pages—forcing their utterance
as the pages stand—coming actually from the this direct urge ‸and developementsdevelopments, of those years and not from any individual epic or lyrical attempt whatever, or from my pen or voice, or any body's special voice. From Out of that supposition, the Book
—or might assume to be considered— an typical emotional autochthonic record and expression freely render'd, and in spirit before letter and from their own radical genesis of and out of these 30 to 35 years—of the deeds and soul⹀developementdevelopment soul and planting evolution of America—and of course, by reflection, more or less of the common spirit and common people of the world. Or it may be I would not ‸ let the great and momentous era of these years, these States, slip away without attempting to arrest in a special printed book some few specimens—even vital breaths—as representatives of it all, from my point of view, and from the midst of it, and at the time...

¶ Then a few additional words yet to this hurried farewell note. In another sense (the warp crossing the woof, and knitted in) the Book is probably a sort of autobiography; an element I have not attempted to specially restrain or erase. ‸As alluded to at ‸beginning I spoke at beginning this edition of I had about got this the Volume well started by the rpinter, when happen'd
a sixth recurrent attack of my war⹀paralysis fell upon me. It has proved the most serious and continued of the whole. I am now uttering Nov: Boughs and printing this Book in my 70th year. To get out the collection—mainly the born results of health, flush life, buoyancy, and happy out-door volition—and to prepare the Boughs—have beguiled my late invalid months, the past summer and fall. ("Are we to be baffled and beaten down then in our old age?" says one white-hair'd fellow remonstratingly to another in a budget of letters I read last night.) . . . . Then I have wanted to leave something markedly personal. I have put my name with pen-and-ink with my own hand in the present Volume. And from engraved or photo'd portraits, taken from life, I have selected some, of different stages, which please me best, (or at any rate displease me least,) and bequeath them at a venture to you, reader with my love.
